card.say: I'll take one tap on a ticket type. The tap goes to the ViewModel, and it asks the price and stock index for that combination. The index was built once from the product data, so the lookup is just a map read. The result comes back on StateFlow, and Compose redraws only the price and stock text. The logic I changed is that calculation: before, every tap recalculated all combinations on the main thread and parsed the JSON again.
card.then: Next: what happens when the product data changes, or the user taps fast.

card.adopted: none
card.heard: other options, why not them, how I knew it worked
card.say: I had three options. First, clear the cache on every index swap. Second, put the index version in the cache key. Third, drop the in-memory cache and read the index directly. I picked the version in the key. Clearing the cache was simple, but every swap threw away good entries.
card.then: Next: the fast-tap case, or how I'd watch this in production.

more: The version in the key also keeps the good entries, so a swap only makes the old ones unreachable. They get removed when they expire or when the size cap is reached. turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the repository saves the intent with its client ID before the request goes out. On Android, what exactly gets written to the local database at that moment, and how does that record change once the server responds?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: Sequence: A confirms on the native screen, the repository saves the intent with its client ID, the API calls the ledger, the ledger moves the money in one transaction, and the result screen shows the server's status
card.constraints: ["Start by clarifying the requirements; define which user path is the MVP"]
card.abandoned: ["MVP is one person sending money to a friend, who sees it arrive; client layers are screen, ViewModel, repository and local database, with a wallet API and ledger behind"]
card.heard: what gets written, and how it changes after the server responds
card.say: At that moment I write one row: the client transfer ID, the payer, the recipient, 8000 cents, and a status of pending. The row goes in before the request leaves, so a crash can't lose it. When the server responds, I update that same row to success or failed, and I store the server's transfer ID. The result screen reads only that row, so it never shows success before the server's record says so.
card.then: Next: what happens when the response is lost, or wait for the interviewer.

updates: The row also keeps the server's transfer ID once it comes back. If the response is lost, the row stays pending, so the app knows the outcome is unknown, not failed. After a restart, I look it up by account and client ID and ask the server for that transfer's status. I only resend the same ID, and the server answers with the original transfer, so the ledger still has one transfer.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: I'd pick the product page at KKday.
Candidate: It's the Android app for a travel platform, and travelers use it to book tours and activities.
Candidate: The problem was speed: when someone tapped a tour, the options and prices took about a second to appear.
Candidate: That's long enough to feel slow.
Candidate: My responsibility started with the Android side.
Candidate: I owned the SKU page features, where users choose packages and options.
Candidate: I rebuilt how the price and stock were calculated, and I brought in Jetpack Compose for the screens.
Candidate: The backend and the product data were other teams' work.
Candidate: When something there was slow or wrong, I raised it with them and agreed on the fix.
Candidate: So my responsibility ended at the app, but I followed the whole flow through to release.
Interviewer: On the KKday product page, you said you rebuilt how price and stock were calculated and brought in Jetpack Compose. Which of those did you personally build versus the team?
Candidate: I built both myself.
Candidate: I rebuilt the price and stock calculation on the phone.
Candidate: I flattened the configuration and built a price and stock index ahead of time.
Candidate: I moved the work to Dispatchers.Default and sent results out through StateFlow.
Candidate: I also brought Compose in and rebuilt the screens with it.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: I'll take one tap on a ticket type.
Candidate: The tap goes to the ViewModel, and it asks the price and stock index for that combination.
Candidate: The index was built once from the product data, so the lookup is just a map read.
Candidate: The result comes back on StateFlow, and Compose redraws only the price and stock text.
Candidate: The logic I changed is that calculation: before, every tap recalculated all combinations on the main thread and parsed the JSON again.
Candidate: The index build runs off the main thread, and if the product data changes at runtime the index has to be rebuilt and swapped atomically so a tap never reads a half-updated map.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a wrong price that only showed up on some dates.
Candidate: It never happened on my test data.
Candidate: I first suspected the index build, because it ran off the main thread.
Candidate: I added a log of the index key and the result for every tap.
Candidate: The log showed the key was right, but the stock value was stale.
Candidate: The real cause was the cache: I kept results in memory and never cleared them when the product data changed.
Candidate: The log showed the key was right, but the stock value was stale, so the index build wasn't the problem.
Candidate: I fixed it by clearing the cache on every index swap, and I added a test with two dates that share the same product.

Interviewer: You said the log showed the key was right but the stock value was stale, and that pointed you to the cache. How did you confirm the stale value actually came from that cache and not from the product data itself being out of date?
Candidate: I checked the product data first.
Candidate: I logged the raw stock value from the backend response, and it was already the new number.
Candidate: So the data was fresh, and the stale value came from my cache.
Candidate: The same product on two dates returned the old stock, which matched the cache key.
Candidate: The cache key didn't include the index version, so a swap left old entries reachable until they expired.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: I had three options.
Candidate: First, clear the cache on every index swap.
Candidate: Second, put the index version in the cache key.
Candidate: Third, drop the in-memory cache and read the index directly.
Candidate: I picked the version in the key.
Candidate: Clearing the cache was simple, but every swap threw away good entries.
Candidate: The version in the key also keeps the good entries, so a swap only makes the old ones unreachable.
Candidate: They get removed when they expire or when the size cap is reached.
Candidate: After release, I went through the booking flow myself on several dates for the same product.
Candidate: The stock matched the backend every time, and switching options felt smooth.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon Securities, I was moving the trading app to modules and MVVM while we kept shipping releases.
Candidate: During testing, I found some old pages had a broken back button with the new navigation.
Candidate: I hadn't checked every page yet, but it could already affect that week's release.
Candidate: So I told the project manager the same day.
Candidate: I gave him two options.
Candidate: First, keep the old pages and move my change to the next release.
Candidate: Second, ship it and accept the risk.
Candidate: I recommended the first one.
Candidate: The two options were: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it this week and test the rest after.
Candidate: He took the first option, so everything else shipped on time.
Candidate: I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change went out in the next release.
Candidate: I also told QA the same day, so they knew what to test first.

Interviewer: You said you recommended keeping the old pages and moving your change to the next release, so what risk were you still willing to accept in that week's release, and who watched the data afterward? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: I was still willing to accept the risk on the old pages.
Candidate: They kept their old navigation, so the back button worked as before.
Candidate: The only risk was that a few pages I hadn't checked might still break.
Candidate: I told QA the same day, so they tested the old pages first.
Candidate: The project manager and I watched the release together.
Candidate: I checked the crash reports in Bugly after it went out.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design, I'd like to check a few things.
Candidate: Who are the users: one person sending money to friends, or a business paying customers?
Candidate: Does the balance sit in our own ledger, or does money move on a bank or card rail?
Candidate: Which currencies do we support?
Candidate: And what must work offline: viewing the balance and history, or also sending?
